topics.title: Complete Safe vs Dangerous NSE Script Reference
topics.content: SAFE SCRIPTS (No Authentication): smb-os-discovery (null session OS info), smb-protocols (SMB version enumeration), smb-security-mode (signing status), smb-vuln-* (all vuln checks use safe probes), ldap-rootdse (anonymous LDAP info), ldap-search (with anonymous bind), ms-sql-info (unauthenticated info), mysql-info (banner/version), http-* (most web scripts), ssh-hostkey, ssh-auth-methods. DANGEROUS SCRIPTS (Cause Lockouts): smb-brute (WILL lock accounts), smb-enum-users with aggressive=true, ldap-brute, ms-sql-brute, mysql-brute, http-form-brute, ssh-brute, vnc-brute, ftp-brute, ALL *-brute scripts. CAUTION SCRIPTS (May Lock with Wrong Args): smb-enum-users (safe in default mode, dangerous with bruteonly), rdp-enum-users (timing-based, may trigger monitoring). RULE: If script name contains 'brute', assume it will cause lockouts. Check script documentation: nmap --script-help <script>

examples.explanation: Check script documentation for lockout warnings

warnings: NEVER run smb-brute in production AD environments
Lockout policies often are 3-5 attempts in 30 minutes
Scripts marked 'intrusive' in categories may still be safe for lockout
'intrusive' != 'causes lockout' - check specifics
best_practices: Test scripts against lab DC first
Coordinate with client on lockout policy before enumeration

topics.title: Multi-Protocol AD Enumeration Without Lockouts
topics.content: AD ENUM STRATEGY: Layer multiple protocols for comprehensive picture without locking accounts. (1) DNS (53): Enumerate via AXFR/IXFR if allowed, or brute common names. No lockout risk. (2) LDAP (389/636): Anonymous bind with ldap-rootdse gets domain name, naming contexts. No auth = no lockout. (3) RPC (135/445): smb-os-discovery, smb-protocols, enum4linux with null session. No lockout. (4) Kerberos (88): AS-REQ username enumeration - Kerberos responds differently to valid vs invalid usernames WITHOUT credentials. Tool: kerbrute. No lockout because no password attempt. (5) SMB Shares: Null session enum4linux -S or smb-enum-shares. No lockout. AVOID: smb-enum-users with any password guessing, smb-brute, ldap-brute. TIMING: Even safe enumeration at high rates may trigger anomaly detection. Add --scan-delay 500ms for stealth.

topics.title: Fragmentation Attacks and MTU Manipulation
topics.content: FRAGMENTATION EVASION: Split probe packets into fragments too small for stateless inspection. --mtu X sets maximum transmission unit, forcing fragmentation. X must be multiple of 8. MECHANISM: TCP header is 20 bytes. With --mtu 8, header splits across 3 fragments. Stateless firewalls/IDS see only first fragment with source/dest IP but incomplete TCP header - may pass traffic. MODERN LIMITATION: Stateful firewalls reassemble before inspection. Most enterprise IDS (Suricata, Snort3) handle fragmentation. STILL WORKS AGAINST: Legacy firewalls, misconfigured iptables, some cloud ACLs, load balancers. DETECTION: Fragmented traffic on unusual ports is suspicious. Normal web traffic rarely fragments. --send-eth bypasses OS fragmentation for full control. ADVANCED: Combine with --data-length to pad fragments, --badsum to test if fragmented packets are checksummed.

topics.title: Decoy Scanning and Source Spoofing
topics.content: DECOY SCANNING (-D): Send probes appearing from multiple source IPs to confuse attribution. YOU are included in the decoy list (use ME keyword). MECHANISM: For each probe, nmap sends identical packets with different source IPs. Target sees scans from many IPs simultaneously. DEFENDER CHALLENGE: All decoys and real scanner look identical. Must investigate all. REQUIREMENTS: Decoy IPs should be (1) up and reachable (or responses reveal the real scanner), (2) not on same subnet as target (easy to verify), (3) plausible for the scan type. RND generates random IPs (often implausible or dead). LIMITATION: Source IP spoofing requires raw sockets (root) and non-egress-filtered network. Most ISPs block spoofed sources (BCP38). Works best on internal pentests. FULL SPOOF (-S): Completely spoof source with no ME. You see no responses. Only useful with idle scan or if you control network path.

topics.title: Writing Custom NSE Scripts
topics.content: NSE SCRIPT STRUCTURE: Written in Lua. Required components: (1) description - what script does, (2) categories - {'safe','intrusive','vuln', etc}, (3) portrule/hostrule - when to run, (4) action - main function. MINIMAL TEMPLATE: description='Custom check'; categories={'safe'}; portrule=function(host,port) return port.number==80 end; action=function(host,port) return 'Port 80 open' end. LIBRARIES: nmap (core), shortport (port matching), stdnse (standard functions), http (web requests), smb (SMB operations), vulns (vulnerability reporting). DEBUGGING: nmap --script-trace shows execution. nmap --script-updatedb after adding scripts. LOCATION: /usr/share/nmap/scripts/ (Linux), custom scripts same directory. EXECUTION: --script=./myscript.nse or copy to scripts dir and run --script=myscript.

examples.explanation: Run custom script from current directory
Update script database after adding new scripts
View help for all HTTP scripts

warnings: Custom scripts can crash nmap if poorly written

Scripts run with nmap's privileges - security implications
best_practices: Start by modifying existing similar script
Use shortport library for clean port matching

topics.title: NSE Script Arguments and Combinations
topics.content: SCRIPT ARGUMENTS: Pass parameters with --script-args. Format: --script-args 'script.arg=value' or --script-args 'arg=value' for global. MULTIPLE ARGS: Comma-separated: --script-args 'http.useragent=Mozilla,smbuser=admin'. ARG FILES: --script-args-file args.txt for complex arguments. COMMON ARGS: creds.global (username:password for all auth scripts), userdb/passdb (wordlist files), http.useragent (custom UA), smbdomain/smbuser/smbpassword (SMB auth). SCRIPT COMBINATIONS: Scripts in same category run in parallel. --script='smb-* and not smb-brute' runs all SMB except brute. Boolean: and, or, not. Categories: --script='safe and discovery'. PERFORMANCE: --script-timeout limits per-script time. --max-parallelism affects script concurrency indirectly.

topics.title: NSE Script Performance Optimization
topics.content: SCRIPT PERFORMANCE ISSUES: NSE scripts can drastically slow scans. http-enum alone can take 30+ seconds per host. TIMEOUTS: --script-timeout 30s limits individual script execution. --host-timeout 10m limits total time per host. PARALLEL SCRIPTS: Scripts in same category MAY run in parallel. Scripts requiring same port run sequentially. REDUCE SCOPE: Use specific scripts, not categories. --script=http-title faster than --script=http-*. NETWORK-INTENSIVE SCRIPTS: http-enum, http-brute, *-brute scripts send many requests. Add delays: --scan-delay 100ms. VERSION DETECTION: -sV runs version scripts. --version-intensity 0-9 controls depth. Lower = faster. MEASURING: --stats-every 10s shows progress. Time with 'time nmap ...' to benchmark. PARALLELISM TUNE: --min-parallelism and --max-parallelism affect port scanning, indirectly affect scripts.

topics.title: Network Signatures for Detecting Nmap Scans
topics.content: NMAP DETECTION SIGNATURES: (1) SYN SCAN: High rate of SYN packets without completing handshake. Signature: >20 SYN to different ports from same source in 1 second. (2) NULL/FIN/XMAS: Illegal flag combinations. NULL = no flags, FIN only = no prior connection, XMAS = FIN+PSH+URG. Any of these = definite scan. (3) VERSION DETECTION: Banner grabs with unusual ordering. Nmap sends probes in specific sequence identifiable via timing pattern. (4) OS DETECTION: Malformed packets like TCP with undefined flag combinations, ICMP with unusual payloads, IP options rarely used in legitimate traffic. (5) NSE SCRIPTS: Script-specific patterns like SMB null session attempts, HTTP requests to non-existent paths. SNORT RULES: 'alert tcp any any -> any any (flags:S; threshold: type threshold, track by_src, count 20, seconds 1; msg:"Possible SYN scan"; sid:1000001;)'. SURICATA: Built-in scan detection in suricata.yaml -> detect-engine -> rule-profiling.

examples.command: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET any (flags:0; msg:"NULL scan detected"; sid:1000010;)
examples.explanation: Snort rule for NULL scan detection

examples.command: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET any (flags:FPU; msg:"XMAS scan detected"; sid:1000011;)
examples.explanation: Snort rule for XMAS scan detection

examples.command: tcpdump -i eth0 'tcp[tcpflags] == tcp-syn' | awk '{print $3}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
examples.explanation: Quick scan detection via SYN counting
Check Suricata logs for scan alerts

warnings: Legitimate vulnerability scanners trigger same signatures
Tune thresholds to environment or face alert fatigue
Encrypted tunnels hide scan patterns
best_practices: Baseline normal SYN rates before setting thresholds
Alert on illegal flag combinations (guaranteed scan)
Correlate source IPs across time windows
Log all scan detections for threat intel

topics.title: Fingerprinting Nmap Itself (Tool Attribution)
topics.content: NMAP LEAVES FINGERPRINTS: Even careful attackers can be identified as using nmap. DETECTION VECTORS: (1) TCP OPTIONS ORDER: Nmap uses MSS,SACK,TS,NOP,WS in specific order, different from OS stacks. (2) WINDOW SIZE: Nmap SYN probes use window size 1024 (common), but OS detection probes use specific values like 65535, 512, etc. rarely seen naturally. (3) TTL VALUES: Nmap defaults may differ from host OS. Linux nmap on Linux sends TTL 64, but scan packets may have TTL 37-64 from probes. (4) TIMING PATTERNS: Script engine has characteristic pause patterns between probe types. (5) USER-AGENT: http-* scripts use 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Nmap Scripting Engine; https://nmap.org/book/nse.html)' unless changed. (6) PROBE SEQUENCES: Version detection sends probes in documented order. COUNTERMEASURE: p0f tool passively fingerprints remote OS including scanner tools. Zeek/Bro logs TCP options for analysis. EVASION: --data-length, --ttl, --spoof-mac change some signatures but not all.

examples.explanation: Run p0f to passively fingerprint all connections

examples.explanation: Find potential nmap SYN scans via TCP options

warnings: Skilled attackers modify nmap source to change fingerprints

Other tools may have similar signatures
best_practices: Log TCP options in firewall/IDS for forensics

Consider honeypots to capture attacker TTPs

topics.title: Defensive Countermeasures and Scan Mitigation
topics.content: LAYERED DEFENSE: (1) PERIMETER: Rate-limit new connections per source IP. iptables: -m recent --update --seconds 60 --hitcount 20 -j DROP. Blocks rapid port scanning. (2) HOST FIREWALL: Default deny inbound. Only allow required ports from authorized sources. (3) PORT KNOCKING: Require specific sequence before port opens. Invisible to scanners. (4) TAR PIT: Slow down attackers with delayed responses. LaBrea, iptables TARPIT target. Wastes scanner time. (5) DECEPTION: Honeypots return fake open ports. Portspoof returns fake banners for all 65535 ports, making scans useless. (6) LOGGING: Log all SYN packets for forensics. iptables -j LOG --log-prefix 'SYN: '. (7) BEHAVIORAL: Fail2ban/CrowdSec auto-block IPs exceeding thresholds. NETWORK: Implement BCP38 (anti-spoofing) to prevent idle scans using your network. CLOUD: AWS Security Groups, Azure NSG - default deny, log with VPC Flow Logs.

examples.command: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --syn -m recent --name portscan --update --seconds 60 --hitcount 20 -j DROP
examples.explanation: Rate limit SYN packets per source IP

best_practices: Alert on scan detection, don't just block

topics.title: When -Pn Makes Things Worse
topics.content: COMMON MISCONCEPTION: 'Host not responding? Use -Pn!' REALITY: -Pn skips host discovery, assuming ALL hosts are up. PROBLEMS: (1) Scanning dead IPs wastes time (default timeout per IP even if dead), (2) Against /24, scanning 254 'hosts' when only 10 are up. (3) Firewall that blocks discovery may also block port scans - you get 'filtered' not 'open'. (4) No host discovery data means missing MAC addresses, reverse DNS. WHEN -Pn HELPS: Single known-live host behind firewall that blocks ICMP/TCP ping. WHEN -Pn HURTS: Subnet scans (massive slowdown), networks with few live hosts, when you need MAC/hostname data. BETTER ALTERNATIVES: (1) Try different discovery: -PS22,80,443 (TCP SYN to common ports), -PA80 (TCP ACK), -PU (UDP). (2) ARP scan if on same subnet: -PR. (3) Reduce timeout: --host-timeout 30s to skip unresponsive hosts faster.

topics.title: Scanning Through Load Balancers and NAT
topics.content: LOAD BALANCER CHALLENGES: (1) Different backend servers have different services. Scan shows union of all backends. (2) Stateless scanning hits different backends per probe - inconsistent results. (3) Health checks may open ports that backends don't serve. (4) Source IP persistence means retries hit same backend - incomplete picture. NAT CHALLENGES: (1) Port forwarding maps external port to different internal port - version detection may be wrong service. (2) Many internal hosts behind one IP - can't enumerate all. (3) Connection tracking affects scan behavior - RST from NAT vs host. DETECTION: Inconsistent banners on same port = load balancer. TTL variations = multiple backends. TECHNIQUES: Run scan multiple times and diff results. Use --max-retries 0 to minimize backend affinity. Add -sV with high intensity to get more banners per backend.

examples.command: for i in {1..5}; do nmap -sV -p 80 --max-retries 0 target -oG scan_$i.gnmap; done && diff scan_*.gnmap

High-intensity version scan for more backend sampling
Check HTTP headers for backend identification

warnings: Single scan may miss services on some backends

topics.title: False Positives and False Negatives Deep Dive
topics.content: FALSE POSITIVES (port shows open but isn't): (1) Stateful firewall RST - firewall sends RST on behalf of closed host, shows as 'closed' (not false positive for closed). (2) Load balancer accepts on port not served - health check port. (3) IDS honeypot responds to all ports. (4) Host replies but service crashed after reply. VERIFICATION: -sV for banner, manual nc/curl test. FALSE NEGATIVES (port is open but shows closed/filtered): (1) Timing too aggressive - packet lost, no retry. Fix: -T3 or lower. (2) Rate limiting - initial responses, then dropped. Fix: --max-rate 100. (3) Stateful firewall - SYN scan works, ACK doesn't. (4) Port filtering based on source IP. (5) Transient service (started after scan passed port). VERIFICATION: Manual test with nc. Scan again with slower timing. Try from different source IP. -sS and -sT may give different results due to OS TCP stack differences. FILTERED REALITY: 'filtered' means no response AND no RST. Could be: firewall drop, packet loss, rate limit, or unreachable host.

topics.title: Asymmetric Routing and MTU Discovery Problems
topics.content: ASYMMETRIC ROUTING: Packets take different paths to and from target. PROBLEMS: (1) Your scan reaches target via path A, response returns via path B. Firewall on path B blocks response - appears filtered. (2) TTL-based techniques (OS fingerprinting) give inconsistent results. (3) Some paths may have different latency - timing calculations wrong. DETECTION: traceroute shows forward path. Check if response TTL differs from expected. Use --reason to see exact response. MTU DISCOVERY ISSUES: PMTUD (Path MTU Discovery) relies on ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages. If blocked, large packets silently dropped. SYMPTOMS: Small packets work, large fail. -sV fails (large probes) but -sS works (small SYN). FIXES: --mtu 1400 to force smaller packets. --send-eth bypasses OS MTU handling. Check path MTU: ping -s 1472 -M do target (Linux).

examples.explanation: Check forward path for routing issues
Test MTU with largest non-fragmented packet
Scan with reduced MTU to avoid fragmentation
Show exact reason for port state

topics.title: Scanning Class A Networks (/8) Efficiently
topics.content: REALITY CHECK: A /8 network = 16.7 million IPs. Full port scan = 16.7M * 65535 = 1 trillion probes. At 1000 pps, that's 31 YEARS. PRACTICAL APPROACH: (1) Use masscan for host discovery (10M pps capable): masscan 10.0.0.0/8 -p 80,443 --rate 100000. (2) Feed live hosts to nmap for detailed scan. (3) Nmap for specific port/service analysis on discovered hosts. NMAP OPTIMIZATION: --min-hostgroup 256, --min-parallelism 100, --max-retries 1, --host-timeout 5m. Use -T5 with --max-rate to prevent network destabilization. OUTPUT MANAGEMENT: Use -oA for every scan. Split targets with --exclude to create resumable chunks. DISTRIBUTED: Use tools like dnmap for multi-scanner coordination. Split target list: split -l 10000 targets.txt target_chunk_. CLOUD: Spin up ephemeral VMs in target's region for low-latency scanning.

examples.explanation: High-speed discovery of common ports across /8
Extract live hosts from masscan output
Detailed scan of discovered hosts with optimized parallelism

topics.title: Output Management and Database Integration
topics.content: ALWAYS USE -oA: Creates .nmap (human), .gnmap (grepable), .xml (structured). XML is key for automation. PARSING XML: Python: from libnmap.parser import NmapParser; report = NmapParser.parse_fromfile('scan.xml'). Ruby: Nmap::XML.new('scan.xml'). DATABASE STORAGE: Import to PostgreSQL/MySQL for correlation across scans. Tools: nmapdb, Sparta, or custom scripts. ELASTICSEARCH: Import for Kibana dashboards: cat scan.xml | nmap-xml-to-json | jq -c '.[]' | while read line; do curl -X POST 'localhost:9200/nmap/_doc' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$line"; done. SPLUNK: Universal Forwarder + nmap XML sourcetype. METASPLOIT: db_import scan.xml loads directly into MSF database. REPORTING: xsltproc with custom XSLT transforms XML to HTML reports. Tools: nmap-bootstrap-xsl for styled reports.

topics.title: Ubuntu/Debian Backporting Explained
topics.content: CRITICAL CONCEPT: Ubuntu and Debian backport security patches to older package versions WITHOUT changing the version number. OpenSSH 7.2p2 on Ubuntu 16.04 may have ALL security patches applied despite showing an 'old' version. This causes massive false positives in vulnerability scanners that rely on version banners. NEVER report vulnerabilities based solely on version numbers for Debian-based systems. Verification required: dpkg -l <package>, apt-cache policy <package>, or check Ubuntu Security Notices.

examples.use_case: Verify OpenSSH patch status on target

warnings: Version banners are UNRELIABLE on Ubuntu/Debian
Scanners report massive false positives
Must verify each 'vulnerability' finding
RHEL/CentOS also backport but differently
best_practices: NEVER report version-based vulns without verification
Use dpkg -l on target if you have access

topics.title: Version Banner vs Actual Patches
topics.content: Version banners reflect upstream version, not security status. Examples: OpenSSH 7.2p2 banner on Ubuntu 18.04 has CVE-2016-6210 patched. Apache 2.4.29 on Ubuntu has CVE-2021-41773 patched. PHP 7.2.24 on Debian has numerous CVEs patched. Verification methods: Package manager queries (dpkg, rpm), security tool outputs (ssh-audit, testssl.sh), vendor security advisories, manual CVE testing.

topics.content: ssh-audit: Comprehensive SSH analysis - algorithms, key exchange, actual CVE status beyond banners. testssl.sh: Deep SSL/TLS testing - all vulnerabilities, cipher analysis, certificate issues. nuclei: Template-based vulnerability verification. topics.title: Packet Fragmentation
topics.content: Splits probes into fragments that some IDS/firewalls fail to reassemble correctly. -f uses 8-byte fragments, -ff uses 16-byte. --mtu sets custom size (multiple of 8). Modern IDS handles fragmentation but combined with other techniques increases evasion. May cause packet loss. Some firewalls block all fragments. Works best for initial SYN scans, not detailed enumeration.
warnings: May not work with version detection/scripts
Some firewalls drop all fragments
Increases scan time
Modern IDS handles fragmentation
best_practices: Test effectiveness before relying on it

topics.title: Decoy Scanning and Spoofing
topics.content: Decoys (-D) send forged packets from multiple IPs: -D decoy1,decoy2,ME,decoy3. RND:10 uses 10 random decoys. Target sees scans from multiple sources. Idle scan (-sI) uses zombie host for complete anonymity - never sends packets from your IP. Source port (--source-port 53) may bypass firewalls allowing DNS. MAC spoofing (--spoof-mac) works on local segment only.

Idle scan needs suitable zombie

best_practices: Use live, diverse IPs as decoys

topics.title: IP ID Sequence Mechanics and Zombie Requirements
topics.content: IDLE SCAN PRINCIPLE: Infer target port state by observing IP ID changes on a 'zombie' host, without sending packets from your IP to target. IP ID is a 16-bit field in IPv4 header used for fragment reassembly. ZOMBIE REQUIREMENT: Must have GLOBALLY INCREMENTING IP ID - each packet the zombie sends increments its IP ID by exactly 1. WHY: (1) You send SYN to TARGET with SPOOFED source = zombie IP, (2) If port OPEN: target sends SYN-ACK to zombie, zombie sends RST (incrementing its IP ID), (3) If port CLOSED: target sends RST to zombie, zombie ignores it (no increment), (4) You probe zombie's IP ID before and after - if it increased by 2 instead of 1, port was open. MODERN CHALLENGE: Most modern OS randomize IP ID per-connection (Linux 4.1+, Windows 10+, BSD). GOOD ZOMBIES: Old printers, IoT devices, legacy Windows (XP/2003), embedded systems. TEST ZOMBIE: nmap -O -v zombie_ip - look for 'IP ID Sequence: Incremental' in output.

topics.title: Idle Scan Failure Modes and Troubleshooting
topics.content: COMMON FAILURES: (1) ALL PORTS SHOW FILTERED: Zombie has random IP ID. Solution: Find different zombie, use -O to verify. (2) INCONSISTENT RESULTS: Zombie has per-host IP ID (common in Linux). Each destination gets different sequence. Solution: Test zombie against target specifically. (3) ZOMBIE PORT CLOSED: If zombie:port specified is closed, scan fails entirely. Solution: Verify port open with direct scan first. (4) STATEFUL FIREWALL: If firewall between zombie and target drops unsolicited SYN-ACKs, zombie never sees response, scan shows all closed. (5) RATE LIMITING: If zombie is rate-limited or has host-based firewall, IP ID increment becomes unpredictable. DEBUGGING: Use --packet-trace to see exact packets. Look for: 'IPID of zombie changed from X to Y'. If Y-X != 1 or 2, zombie is unsuitable. ALTERNATIVE: If no good zombie exists, consider -sS with decoys (-D) instead for partial anonymity.

QUERIES: hosts - list discovered hosts. services -p 445 - find SMB. vulns - list vulnerability findings. HOST NOTES: nmap script output stored in notes table: notes -t nmap.* shows all nmap-sourced notes. WORKSPACE: Use 'workspace -a projectname' to organize. Keeps client data separate.

topics.title: Parsing Nmap Output for Automation

Format: Host: IP (hostname) Ports: port/state/proto/svc/version. COMMON EXTRACTIONS: IPs with open port: grep '/open/' scan.gnmap | awk '{print $2}'. Open ports for IP: grep 'Host: 10.0.0.1' scan.gnmap | grep -oP '\d+/open'. XML PARSING: Most complete data. Python: python-nmap or libnmap libraries. jq for quick queries after converting to JSON. PYTHON EXAMPLE: from libnmap.parser import NmapParser; report = NmapParser.parse_fromfile('scan.xml'); for host in report.hosts: print(host.address, [s.port for s in host.services if s.state == 'open']). JQ EXAMPLE: nmap ... -oX - | xq '.nmaprun.host[]' (requires yq/xq for XML to JSON).

topics.title: CI/CD and Automated Scanning Pipelines
topics.content: AUTOMATED SCANNING USE CASES: (1) Baseline scanning - detect new hosts/services. (2) Compliance verification - ensure only allowed ports open. (3) Change detection - diff against previous scans. (4) Vulnerability monitoring - regular vuln script runs. PIPELINE INTEGRATION: Jenkins/GitLab CI/GitHub Actions can run nmap in containers. Use --open to reduce output, -oX for parsing. DIFF SCANNING: ndiff compares two scans: ndiff baseline.xml current.xml shows changes. ALERTING: Parse output for unexpected ports, pipe to Slack/PagerDuty. EXIT CODES: nmap returns 0 on success. Use $? to detect failures in scripts. CONTAINERIZED: docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/data instrumentisto/nmap -oX /data/scan.xml target. SCHEDULING: Cron for regular scans. Add timestamp to output: -oX scan_$(date +%Y%m%d).xml.

topics.title: Diagnosing Slow Scans and Bottlenecks
topics.content: COMMON BOTTLENECKS: (1) DNS resolution - each host resolved serially by default. Fix: -n to skip DNS, or --dns-servers with fast resolver. (2) Host discovery - waiting for timeouts on dead hosts. Fix: -Pn only for single hosts, otherwise faster discovery methods. (3) Version detection - probes take time. Fix: --version-intensity 2 or lower. (4) Script execution - NSE scripts vary widely. Fix: specific scripts not categories. (5) Retries on filtered ports - waiting for responses that won't come. Fix: --max-retries 1. (6) Parallelism too low - nmap being conservative. Fix: --min-hostgroup 64, --min-parallelism 50. DIAGNOSIS: Use --stats-every 5s to watch progress. Identify which phase is slow. Use -v for verbose progress. Check system resources: CPU, memory, network bandwidth.

topics.title: Debugging NSE Script Failures
topics.content: SCRIPT FAILURE MODES: (1) Script doesn't run - portrule/hostrule not matched. Check with --script-help. (2) Script errors - Lua runtime errors. Use -d2 or higher for details. (3) Script timeout - exceeded --script-timeout. Increase or check network issues. (4) Script returns nil - conditions not met for output. Check with --script-trace. (5) Wrong output - script logic issue or target non-standard. DEBUG TOOLS: --script-trace shows script execution details. -d -d (debug level 2) shows Lua errors. --script-help scriptname shows requirements. nmap --script-updatedb if new script not found. COMMON ISSUES: Missing dependencies (library not installed). Wrong script arguments (check --script-help). Target not responding as expected. Firewall blocking script probes.

topics.title: Handling Network Instability and High Latency
topics.content: HIGH LATENCY SCENARIOS: Satellite links (500ms+ RTT), international VPN, Tor scanning, multi-hop pivots. PACKET LOSS SCENARIOS: Wireless networks, congested links, aggressive rate limiting. TIMING ADJUSTMENTS: --initial-rtt-timeout 1s (up from 1s default). --max-rtt-timeout 10s (up from 10s max). --min-rtt-timeout 500ms (up from 100ms). --max-retries 5 (up from 10 for filtered). --host-timeout 60m for complete unreliable hosts. --scan-delay 500ms to avoid overwhelming slow links. DETECTION: ping -c 100 target | grep 'packet loss' to measure. traceroute to identify slow hops. --reason shows why ports classified as filtered (timeouts). SATELLITE SPECIFIC: 500-700ms RTT is normal. Jitter high. Use -T2 or lower. Expect scans to take 10x longer. REALISTIC EXPECTATIONS: Full port scan over satellite may take hours. Prioritize ports ruthlessly.

topics.title: Scope Verification and Target Validation
topics.content: SCOPE VERIFICATION IS CRITICAL: Scanning unauthorized targets is illegal in most jurisdictions. BEFORE SCANNING: (1) Verify target IP ranges in writing. (2) Confirm DNS names resolve to authorized IPs. (3) Check cloud IPs haven't rotated to another customer. (4) Verify hosting provider approval if required (AWS, Azure, shared hosting). TECHNIQUES: Resolve all targets before scanning: nmap -sL --resolve-all targets.txt. Use --exclude and --excludefile for out-of-scope ranges. Verify ownership: whois, ASN lookup, reverse DNS. DOCUMENTATION: Screenshot authorization documents. Log all scope verification steps. Timestamp all scans. CLOUD DANGER: Cloud IPs change frequently. 10.0.0.5 you scanned last week may be different customer today. Always re-verify cloud targets. SHARED HOSTING: One IP may host hundreds of sites. Authorization for site X doesn't authorize scanning all sites on that IP.

topics.title: Evidence Preservation and Chain of Custody
topics.content: EVIDENCE STANDARDS: Scan results may be used in legal proceedings, compliance audits, or incident response. PRESERVATION REQUIREMENTS: (1) Immutable timestamps - use -oA with date in filename. (2) Hash outputs - sha256sum scan.xml immediately after scan. (3) Full command line - log exact nmap command used. (4) Environment documentation - scanner IP, nmap version, OS. CHAIN OF CUSTODY: Document who ran scan, from where, when, and how results were stored. Use write-once storage (append-only logs, WORM storage). INTEGRITY: Store original files without modification. If processing needed, keep originals separate. REPORTING: Include methodology in reports - exact commands, timing, any issues encountered. LEGAL: Consult counsel before penetration testing. Understand local laws (CFAA in US, CMA in UK, etc.).

topics.title: Notification and Coordination Requirements
topics.content: WHO TO NOTIFY: (1) Client IT/Security - always, with scheduled windows. (2) ISP/Hosting provider - if their terms require it. (3) MSSP/SOC - so they don't respond to your 'attack'. (4) Third-party vendors - if their infrastructure in scope. WHAT TO DOCUMENT IN ROE: (1) Authorized targets (IP ranges, domains). (2) Authorized techniques (scanning yes, exploitation TBD). (3) Timing windows (business hours, maintenance windows). (4) Emergency contacts (who to call if something breaks). (5) Stop conditions (when to halt testing). CLOUD PROVIDERS: AWS - no notification needed for most services you own, but check current policy. Azure - similar. GCP - similar. All prohibit scanning resources you don't own. INCIDENT RISK: Even authorized scans may trigger automated responses. Coordinate with SOC to prevent IP blocks, log correlation confusion, or incident response activation.

topics.title: Nmap Syntax and Target Specification
topics.content: Nmap (Network Mapper) is the industry-standard network discovery and security auditing tool. The basic command structure: nmap [Scan Type] [Options] [Target]. Target specification supports: single IPs (192.168.1.1), hostnames (target.example.com), CIDR notation (192.168.1.0/24 for 256 hosts), ranges (192.168.1.1-50), and octet ranges (192.168.0-255.1). Use -iL to read targets from file. Use --exclude and --excludefile to skip sensitive systems. Nmap performs host discovery before port scanning unless -Pn is specified.

topics.title: When to Use Nmap vs Other Tools
topics.content: Nmap excels at accuracy and deep enumeration but isn't always fastest. Masscan scans entire Internet in minutes but sacrifices accuracy. RustScan combines Masscan speed with Nmap integration. Zmap is for Internet-scale research. Use Nmap when you need: accurate version detection, vulnerability scanning via NSE, OS fingerprinting, stealth capabilities, or comprehensive analysis. Common workflow: Masscan for discovery, Nmap for deep enumeration of identified hosts.

topics.title: Port Ranges and Lists
topics.content: The -p flag specifies ports. Single: -p 22. Range: -p 1-1000. List: -p 22,80,443. Combined: -p 22,80,443,1000-2000. Full scan: -p- (all 65535). Protocol prefix: -p T:22,80,U:53,161 for TCP/UDP mix. --top-ports N scans N most common ports. --exclude-ports removes specific ports. Develop standard port sets: web (80,443,8080,8443), Windows (135,139,445,3389,5985), databases (1433,1521,3306,5432,27017).

topics.title: Fast Scan vs Full Scan Strategies
topics.content: Fast scan (-F) reduces to 100 ports vs default 1000. Full scan (-p-) covers all 65535. Strategy depends on time, stealth, and thoroughness needs. External perimeters: be thorough. Large internal networks: fast initial sweep, then full scan interesting hosts. Hybrid: --top-ports 3000 balances speed and coverage. Multi-phase: -F across network, identify targets, -p- those hosts.

topics.title: IPv6 Scanning Challenges and Techniques
topics.content: IPv6 SCANNING CHALLENGES: (1) Address space is 2^128 - brute force host discovery impossible. A /64 subnet has 18 quintillion addresses. (2) No ARP - uses ICMPv6 Neighbor Discovery instead. (3) Multiple addresses per host (link-local fe80::, global, temporary privacy addresses). (4) Many networks are dual-stack - scan both protocols. DISCOVERY TECHNIQUES: (1) Multicast ping: ping6 ff02::1%eth0 reaches all link-local nodes. (2) DNS enumeration: AAAA records reveal IPv6 addresses. (3) IPv4 mapping: Convert known IPv4 hosts to IPv6 (stateless addressing uses MAC). (4) Traffic sniffing: Passive discovery of active IPv6 hosts. NMAP IPv6: Use -6 flag. Host discovery uses ICMPv6 echo, TCP SYN, UDP. Many firewalls neglect IPv6 rules - potential bypass. COMMON PATTERNS: ::1 (localhost), fe80::/10 (link-local), 2000::/3 (global unicast), ff00::/8 (multicast).

topics.title: SCTP Scanning for Telecom Networks
topics.content: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol): Used in telecom signaling (SS7/SIGTRAN, Diameter, LTE), some databases, and WebRTC. Multi-homing and multi-streaming protocol. SCAN TYPES: -sY (SCTP INIT scan): Sends INIT chunk, open port responds with INIT-ACK, closed with ABORT. Equivalent to TCP SYN scan. -sZ (SCTP COOKIE-ECHO scan): More stealthy, sends COOKIE-ECHO which is dropped by open ports (no state), ABORT from closed. COMMON SCTP PORTS: 2905 (M3UA), 2945 (M2PA), 3868 (Diameter), 9899 (SCTP testing), 36412 (S1AP/LTE). DETECTION: SCTP requires kernel support. Check: cat /proc/net/protocols | grep SCTP. If missing, modprobe sctp. Windows nmap cannot do SCTP scans (no kernel support). IMPORTANT: SCTP is rare outside telecom. Finding it indicates telecom infrastructure, VoLTE, or specialized systems.

topics.title: Industrial Control Systems (ICS/SCADA) Scanning
topics.content: ICS/SCADA PROTOCOLS: Industrial systems use specialized protocols rarely seen in IT networks. MODBUS (502/tcp): Serial protocol over TCP for PLCs. NSE: modbus-discover identifies device info. S7COMM (102/tcp): Siemens S7 PLC protocol. NSE: s7-info extracts hardware/firmware details. BACNET (47808/udp): Building automation. NSE: bacnet-info discovers BACnet devices. DNP3 (20000/tcp): Power grid SCADA. NSE: dnp3-info for device identification. ENIP/CIP (44818/tcp): Rockwell/Allen-Bradley industrial ethernet. NSE: enip-info. CRITICAL WARNING: ICS devices are fragile. Aggressive scanning can crash PLCs, causing physical damage or safety issues. NEVER scan production ICS without explicit authorization and safety measures. Use passive discovery when possible.

topics.title: SOCKS Proxy Limitations for Raw Packet Scans
topics.content: CRITICAL: SOCKS proxies operate at OSI Layer 5 (session layer) and can ONLY proxy established TCP connections, NOT raw IP packets. This is why -sS (SYN scan) FAILS through SOCKS: (1) SYN scans require CAP_NET_RAW to craft custom TCP headers with only SYN flag set, (2) SOCKS protocol has no mechanism to encapsulate arbitrary IP packets - it only understands CONNECT requests for TCP streams, (3) When nmap sends a raw SYN packet, the local kernel has no route through the SOCKS proxy. SOLUTION: Use -sT (TCP connect scan) which uses the OS connect() syscall to establish full TCP connections. The kernel routes these through proxychains normally. TRADE-OFFS: -sT is slower (full 3-way handshake vs half-open), more detectable (connection fully established), and leaves logs on target (accept() called). ALSO INCOMPATIBLE: -sU (UDP), -sA (ACK), -sW (Window), -sM (Maimon), -sN/-sF/-sX (NULL/FIN/Xmas) - ALL require raw sockets.

topics.title: SSH Tunneling vs SOCKS vs VPN for Scanning
topics.content: THREE MAIN PIVOT METHODS: (1) SSH SOCKS Proxy (-D): Creates SOCKS4a/5 proxy on local port, requires proxychains, only TCP connect scans work, simple to set up. Command: ssh -D 9050 user@pivot. (2) SSH Local Port Forward (-L): Forwards specific local port to remote host:port, no proxychains needed, nmap connects directly to localhost:port, but only ONE target port at a time. Command: ssh -L 8445:internal:445 user@pivot then nmap -sT -p 8445 localhost. (3) VPN/Tun (sshuttle, OpenVPN, WireGuard): Creates Layer 3 tunnel, ALL scan types work including -sS/-sU, nmap sees real internal IPs, most transparent but requires root on pivot or VPN server. COMPARISON: SOCKS is easiest but most limited. Local forward is surgical but tedious for many ports. VPN is most powerful but hardest to set up in pentest scenarios. EXPERT TIP: Use sshuttle for quick Layer 3 tunnel without full VPN: sshuttle -r user@pivot 10.0.0.0/8 --dns

topics.title: Multi-Hop Pivoting and Scan Performance
topics.content: MULTI-HOP REALITY: Each pivot adds 50-200ms latency. A double-pivot (you -> DMZ -> internal -> target) means 100-400ms round-trip MINIMUM. Nmap default timeouts assume <100ms latency. CRITICAL ADJUSTMENTS: (1) Increase --host-timeout to 30m or higher, (2) Use --max-retries 3 or higher, (3) Set --min-rtt-timeout 500ms and --max-rtt-timeout 5s, (4) Reduce parallelism with --max-parallelism 5 to prevent proxy overload. PROXYCHAINS CHAINING: Edit /etc/proxychains.conf with multiple SOCKS proxies in order - traffic flows through each sequentially. Use 'strict_chain' mode for predictable routing. DOUBLE SSH: ssh -J user@hop1 user@hop2 -D 9050 creates SOCKS through two SSH hops. LATENCY KILL: A /24 subnet scan that takes 5 minutes direct can take 2+ HOURS through double pivot. Prioritize port selection ruthlessly.

topics.title: TCP SYN Scan (-sS)
topics.content: Default scan type with root privileges. Sends SYN packet, analyzes response without completing connection. SYN-ACK = open, RST = closed, no response = filtered. Called 'half-open' because connection never completes. Faster than TCP Connect, less logging on target. Requires root for raw socket access. Modern IDS still detects SYN scans but technique remains valuable for speed and reliability.

topics.title: TCP Connect Scan (-sT)
topics.content: Completes full TCP three-way handshake. Default when running without root. Uses OS connect() system call. Connections fully logged by target. Necessary for scanning through SOCKS proxies (proxychains). Slower than SYN scan. Use when root unavailable or proxy required.

topics.content: Essential for complete assessment - critical services use UDP: DNS (53), SNMP (161), TFTP (69), NFS. UDP is connectionless - open ports often don't respond. ICMP port unreachable = closed, no response = open|filtered. Very slow due to ICMP rate limiting. Focus on high-value UDP ports rather than full scans. Combine with TCP: -sS -sU -p T:1-1000,U:53,161.

topics.title: FIN, NULL, and Xmas Scans
topics.content: Exploit RFC 793: closed ports must respond with RST to packets without SYN/RST/ACK flags. Open ports should ignore. FIN scan (-sF) sends FIN only. NULL scan (-sN) sends no flags. Xmas scan (-sX) sends FIN+PSH+URG. Main advantage: may bypass firewalls that only block SYN. CRITICAL: Does NOT work against Windows - they respond RST to everything. Only useful against Unix/Linux. Can only distinguish closed from open|filtered.

topics.title: ACK and Window Scans
topics.content: NOT for finding open ports - for mapping firewall rules. ACK scan (-sA) sends ACK packets. RST response = unfiltered (reaches host). No response = filtered. Cannot determine if ports are open. Window scan (-sW) examines RST window size for open/closed hints (unreliable, OS-dependent). Use to map what firewall allows, then SYN scan unfiltered ports.

topics.title: SSH Username Enumeration via Timing (CVE-2018-15473)
topics.content: CVE-2018-15473 MECHANISM: OpenSSH before 7.7 has timing difference in authentication response. When client sends auth request: (1) VALID username: Server loads user's hashed password, compares against provided password, then rejects - takes ~50-100ms, (2) INVALID username: Server immediately rejects without password lookup - takes ~10-30ms. EXPLOIT: Send malformed auth packet that causes server to reveal timing before auth completes. NMAP SCRIPT: ssh-auth-methods was NOT designed for this. Use dedicated tools: ssh-user-enum.py, or Metasploit auxiliary/scanner/ssh/ssh_enumusers. CRITICAL: Even timing-based enum triggers fail2ban because connection is established. Each probe = 1 SSH connection logged. Ban threshold (usually 5) reached quickly. MITIGATION CHECK: dpkg -l openssh-server | grep 7.[7-9] (7.7+ patched). Ubuntu 18.04+ backported fix.

topics.title: Response Timing Analysis for Service Fingerprinting
topics.content: TIMING AS FINGERPRINT: Beyond version strings, response timing reveals implementation details. TECHNIQUES: (1) TCP handshake timing: Time between SYN and SYN-ACK varies by OS/implementation. Linux ~0.5ms local, Windows ~1-2ms. (2) Application response timing: Database query time reveals backend. Instant response = cached, 100ms+ = disk query, 500ms+ = complex join. (3) Error handling timing: Invalid input processed faster than valid-but-wrong = indicates input validation logic. (4) Crypto timing: Weak implementations leak key bits through decrypt time. NMAP TIMING: Use --min-rtt-timeout and --initial-rtt-timeout to measure baseline. Script timing: capture output with timestamps. ADVANCED: Use hping3 for microsecond precision TCP timing. DEFENSE EVASION: Consistent timing = protection. Add random delays to mask processing time.

T2 (Polite): 0.4 sec intervals, reduces network load. T3 (Normal): Default, balanced. T4 (Aggressive): Faster, assumes reliable network, good for internal.
